questions.q: What are the three main layers of the Earth?
questions.fact: The core is split into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

questions.q: Which layer of the Earth is the thickest?
questions.fact: The mantle is about 2,900 kilometers thick.

questions.q: Is Earth's outer core solid or liquid?
questions.fact: The swirling liquid iron in the outer core creates Earth's magnetic field.

questions.q: About how hot is Earth's inner core?
questions.fact: That is roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun.

questions.q: Why is Earth's inner core solid even though it is so hot?
choices: The huge pressure squeezes it solid
questions.fact: The pressure at the center of Earth is millions of times the air pressure at the surface.

questions.q: About how deep is the deepest hole people have ever drilled into Earth?
questions.fact: The Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia reached about 12.2 kilometers, still only in the crust.

questions.q: How thick is Earth's crust under the oceans compared with under the continents?
choices: There is no crust under oceans
questions.fact: Ocean crust is often about 7 kilometers thick, while continental crust is usually 30 to 50 kilometers.

questions.q: What is the name for molten rock that comes out onto Earth's surface?
questions.fact: Lava can be hotter than 1,000 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Which type of rock forms from layers of sand, mud or shells pressed together?
questions.fact: Most fossils are found in sedimentary rock.

questions.q: Which type of rock forms when other rocks are changed by heat and pressure?
questions.fact: Marble is metamorphic rock that started out as limestone.

questions.q: What is the slow cycle of rocks changing from one type to another called?
questions.fact: The rock cycle can take millions of years to complete.

questions.q: Which rock is so light and full of air bubbles that it can float on water?
questions.fact: Pumice forms when bubbly lava cools very quickly.

questions.q: Which shiny black volcanic glass forms when lava cools very fast?
questions.fact: Ancient people chipped obsidian into very sharp knives and arrowheads.

questions.q: Which speckled igneous rock is often used for kitchen countertops?
questions.fact: Granite forms when magma cools slowly deep underground.

questions.q: Which metamorphic rock is often used for statues, like Michelangelo's David?
questions.fact: Michelangelo carved David from a single block of marble from Carrara, Italy.

questions.q: Which rock splits into thin flat sheets and was used for chalkboards and roofs?
questions.fact: Slate forms from mudstone squeezed by heat and pressure.

questions.q: Which soft white sedimentary rock is made from tiny sea creature shells?
questions.fact: The White Cliffs of Dover in England are made of chalk.

questions.q: Which dark volcanic rock makes up most of the ocean floor?
questions.fact: Hawaii's islands are built mostly from basalt lava.

questions.q: What is the softest mineral on the Mohs hardness scale?
questions.fact: Talc is so soft you can scratch it with your fingernail.

questions.q: How many steps are on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness?
questions.fact: Diamond is a 10 and talc is a 1.

questions.q: Which common mineral makes up most beach sand?
questions.fact: Quartz is hard and does not wear away easily, so it lasts as sand.

questions.q: Which mineral is known as fool's gold because it looks like gold?
questions.fact: Pyrite is harder than gold and makes sparks when struck against steel.

questions.q: What do you call a hollow rock lined with crystals inside?
questions.fact: Geodes often look plain and round on the outside.

questions.q: What is the name for natural solid substances with a crystal structure, like quartz and salt?
questions.fact: Rocks are made of one or more minerals.

questions.q: What are the icicle-like rock formations that hang from cave ceilings called?
questions.fact: Stalactites hold tight to the ceiling, and stalagmites might grow up from the ground.

questions.q: What are the rock formations that grow up from cave floors called?
questions.fact: When a stalactite and stalagmite meet, they form a column.

questions.q: What mainly carves out most caves in limestone?
questions.fact: Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide, which makes a weak acid that slowly dissolves limestone.

questions.q: What is the longest known cave system in the world?
questions.fact: As of 2025, more than 680 kilometers of Mammoth Cave in Kentucky have been mapped.

questions.q: Which cave in Vietnam has the largest known cave passage, with its own jungle inside?
questions.fact: Son Doong is big enough to fit a whole city block of skyscrapers.

questions.q: What is a hole in the ground that suddenly forms when underground rock dissolves and collapses?
questions.fact: Florida has many sinkholes because of the limestone under the ground.

questions.q: What is the process of rock being broken down by wind, water and ice called?
questions.fact: Weathering breaks rock, and erosion carries the pieces away.

questions.q: What is the moving away of rocks and soil by wind, water or ice called?
questions.fact: The Grand Canyon was carved by erosion from the Colorado River.

questions.q: What is it called when rivers drop sand and mud in a new place?
questions.fact: River deltas form through deposition where rivers meet the sea.

questions.q: What is a wide, flat-topped hill with steep sides, common in the American Southwest?
questions.fact: Mesa means table in Spanish.

questions.q: What is a deep valley with steep sides, often carved by a river?
questions.fact: Canyons can take millions of years to form.

questions.q: What shape of valley do glaciers usually carve?
questions.fact: Rivers usually carve V-shaped valleys.

questions.q: What is a hill of sand piled up by the wind called?
questions.fact: Some sand dunes in the Sahara are over 150 meters tall.

questions.q: What is an area with plenty of water in a desert, where plants grow, called?
questions.fact: Oases often form where underground water comes up to the surface.

questions.q: What is a mirage?
choices: A trick of light that looks like water far away
questions.fact: Mirages happen when hot air near the ground bends light.

questions.q: What is the boundary where two tectonic plates move apart called?
questions.fact: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a divergent boundary under the ocean.

questions.q: What is the boundary where two tectonic plates push together called?
questions.fact: The Himalayas formed where the Indian plate pushes into the Eurasian plate.

questions.q: Which famous fault in California is where two plates slide past each other?
questions.fact: The San Andreas Fault runs about 1,200 kilometers through California.

questions.q: About how fast do tectonic plates move?
choices: About as fast as fingernails grow
questions.fact: Most plates move between about 2 and 10 centimeters a year.

questions.q: Which mountain range is still growing taller because two plates are pushing together?
questions.fact: Mount Everest rises a few millimeters every year.

questions.q: Who proposed the idea of continental drift in 1912?
questions.fact: Wegener noticed that the coasts of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces.

questions.q: What is the point on Earth's surface right above where an earthquake starts called?
questions.fact: The point underground where the earthquake actually starts is called the focus or hypocenter.

questions.q: Which scale is used to measure an earthquake's magnitude today?
questions.fact: Each step up on the scale means about 32 times more energy released.

questions.q: What was the most powerful earthquake ever recorded?
questions.fact: The 1960 Valdivia earthquake had a magnitude of about 9.5.

questions.q: What are the smaller earthquakes that come after a big one called?
questions.fact: Aftershocks can keep happening for weeks or even years.

questions.q: What is a giant ocean wave caused by an undersea earthquake called?
questions.fact: Tsunami is a Japanese word meaning harbor wave.

questions.q: What should you do indoors during an earthquake?
questions.fact: Getting under a sturdy table protects you from falling objects.

questions.q: What is a warning sign of a tsunami at the beach?
choices: The sea suddenly pulls far back from the shore
questions.fact: If the water suddenly drains away, people should move to high ground right away.

questions.q: What is the opening in Earth's crust where lava and gas come out called?
questions.fact: The word volcano comes from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire.

questions.q: What is the bowl-shaped hole at the top of a volcano called?
questions.fact: A very large crater formed when a volcano collapses is called a caldera.

questions.q: What is the large bowl formed when a volcano collapses after a huge eruption?
questions.fact: Crater Lake in Oregon fills a caldera made about 7,700 years ago.

questions.q: What do we call a volcano that has not erupted in a very long time and is not expected to erupt again?
questions.fact: A dormant volcano is only sleeping and could erupt again.

questions.q: What kind of broad, gently sloping volcano is Mauna Loa in Hawaii?
questions.fact: Shield volcanoes get their name because they look like a warrior's shield lying on the ground.

questions.q: Which volcano in Italy buried the city of Pompeii?
questions.fact: Vesuvius is still an active volcano near the city of Naples.

questions.q: Which volcano in Washington State erupted in 1980, blowing off its top?
questions.fact: The eruption lowered the mountain by about 400 meters.

questions.q: Which Indonesian volcano's 1883 eruption was heard thousands of kilometers away?
questions.fact: It is often called one of the loudest sounds in recorded history.

questions.q: Which Indonesian volcano erupted in 1815 and caused the Year Without a Summer?
questions.fact: Ash in the sky cooled the planet, and snow fell in New England in June 1816.

questions.q: Which is the tallest mountain on Earth when measured from its base on the ocean floor?
questions.fact: Mauna Kea in Hawaii is over 10,000 meters from base to top, but most of it is underwater.

questions.q: Which point on Earth is farthest from the planet's center?
questions.fact: Earth bulges at the equator, so Chimborazo in Ecuador sticks out the farthest.

questions.q: Which is the deepest part of the ocean?
choices: The bottom of the Red Sea
Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench
questions.fact: It is about 11 kilometers deep, deeper than Mount Everest is tall.

questions.q: Who were the first people to reach the bottom of the Mariana Trench, in 1960?
questions.fact: They dove in a vessel called the Trieste, and filmmaker James Cameron made a solo dive there in 2012.

questions.q: What is the world's longest mountain range, mostly underwater?
questions.fact: The Mid-Ocean Ridge winds about 65,000 kilometers around the globe.

questions.q: What percentage of Earth's surface is covered by water?
questions.fact: That is why Earth is often called the Blue Planet.

questions.q: About what percent of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans?
questions.fact: Only about 3 percent of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice.

questions.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water stored?
questions.fact: The Antarctic ice sheet alone holds most of the world's fresh water.

questions.q: Why is the ocean salty?
choices: Rivers carry dissolved minerals from rocks into the sea
questions.fact: When ocean water evaporates, the salt stays behind, so it builds up over time.

questions.q: How many oceans does Earth have, as most geographers count them today?
questions.fact: They are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic oceans.

questions.q: Which ocean is the second largest?
questions.fact: The Atlantic Ocean is getting wider by a few centimeters each year.

questions.q: Which warm ocean current flows from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic toward Europe?
questions.fact: The Gulf Stream helps keep parts of Western Europe milder than other places as far north.

questions.q: What is the name for the rising and falling of the sea level twice a day?
questions.fact: Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes.

questions.q: What causes most ocean waves?
questions.fact: The longer and harder the wind blows, the bigger the waves get.

questions.q: What is the largest coral reef system in the world?
questions.fact: It stretches over 2,000 kilometers and can be seen from space.

questions.q: What happens to coral when the water gets too warm?
choices: It can turn white, called coral bleaching
questions.fact: Bleached coral has lost the tiny algae that give it food and color.

questions.q: What is the zone of the ocean too deep for any sunlight to reach called?
questions.fact: In the midnight zone, the only light comes from glowing animals.

questions.q: What are hot springs on the deep sea floor where strange creatures live called?
questions.fact: Giant tube worms near vents live without sunlight, getting food from bacteria.

questions.q: What is the longest river in the world?
questions.fact: Some scientists argue the Amazon is longer, depending on how its source is measured.

questions.q: What is the place where a river begins called?
questions.fact: The place where a river ends, usually at a sea or lake, is called its mouth.

questions.q: What is the area of land that drains into one river called?
questions.fact: Everything that falls on a watershed eventually drains toward the same river.

questions.q: What is an underground layer of rock that holds water called?
questions.fact: Wells pump water up from aquifers.

questions.q: What do we call a swampy, wet land area like a marsh or bog?
questions.fact: Wetlands soak up floodwater like a giant sponge.

questions.q: What is the large wetland in southern Florida famous for alligators called?
questions.fact: The Everglades is sometimes called a river of grass.

questions.q: What are the large areas with similar climate, plants and animals, like deserts and rainforests, called?
questions.fact: Major biomes include tundra, desert, grassland, forest and rainforest.

questions.q: What is the huge forest of evergreen trees across Canada, Scandinavia and Russia called?
questions.fact: The taiga, or boreal forest, is the largest land biome on Earth.

questions.q: What is the grassland with scattered trees in Africa called?
questions.fact: Lions, zebras and elephants live on the African savanna.

questions.q: What are the grasslands of North America called?
questions.fact: Huge herds of bison once roamed the prairies.

questions.q: What do we call ground that stays frozen all year in very cold places?
questions.fact: As permafrost thaws, it can release greenhouse gases.

questions.q: What is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth?
questions.fact: The Amazon is home to about one in ten known species on Earth.

questions.q: What is the top layer of a rainforest, where most branches and leaves spread out, called?
questions.fact: The canopy can block so much light that the forest floor is dark even at noon.

questions.q: What is a desert?
choices: A place that gets very little rain
A place covered in sand only
questions.fact: Antarctica counts as a desert because it gets so little snow and rain.

questions.q: What is the largest desert in the world, counting cold deserts?
questions.fact: The Sahara is the largest hot desert.

questions.q: Which desert in South America is one of the driest places on Earth?
questions.fact: Some weather stations in the Atacama have almost never recorded rain.

questions.q: In which desert is Death Valley, one of the hottest places on Earth?
questions.fact: Death Valley in California recorded about 56.7 degrees Celsius in 1913.

questions.q: What is the name of a big desert in Mongolia and China famous for dinosaur fossils?
questions.fact: The first dinosaur egg nests were found in the Gobi in the 1920s.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies weather called?
questions.fact: Meteorologists study the atmosphere, not meteors.

questions.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
choices: Weather is day to day, climate is the long-term pattern
questions.fact: You could say climate is what you expect and weather is what you get.

questions.q: What is the layer of gases around Earth called?
questions.fact: Most of the atmosphere's air is in the lowest 16 kilometers or so.

questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere do most planes fly in or just above?
questions.fact: Planes fly high to stay above most of the bumpy weather.

questions.q: In which layer of the atmosphere do most meteors burn up?
questions.fact: The mesosphere is the coldest layer of the atmosphere.

questions.q: What instrument measures wind speed?
questions.fact: Many anemometers have spinning cups that turn faster in stronger wind.

questions.q: What instrument shows which way the wind is blowing?
questions.fact: A wind vane points toward the direction the wind is coming from.

questions.q: What instrument measures how much rain has fallen?
questions.fact: A rain gauge is basically a cup with measuring marks.

questions.q: What scale describes wind strength by what it does, from calm to hurricane?
questions.fact: It was created in 1805 by Francis Beaufort, a British navy officer.

questions.q: Which scale rates hurricanes from Category 1 to Category 5?
questions.fact: A Category 5 hurricane has winds of at least 252 kilometers per hour.

questions.q: Which scale is used to rate tornadoes by their damage?
questions.fact: It goes from EF0, the weakest, to EF5, the most violent.

questions.q: What are high, thin, wispy clouds made of ice crystals called?
questions.fact: Cirrus means curl of hair in Latin.

questions.q: What are puffy white clouds that look like cotton balls called?
questions.fact: Cumulus means heap or pile in Latin.

questions.q: What are flat, gray clouds that cover the sky like a blanket called?
questions.fact: Stratus clouds often bring drizzle or gloomy days.

questions.q: What is fog?
questions.fact: Fog forms when air near the ground cools and its water vapor condenses.

questions.q: What are clouds made of?
choices: Tiny water droplets or ice crystals
questions.fact: A puffy cumulus cloud can weigh as much as about 100 elephants.

questions.q: What is the water that collects on grass on cool mornings called?
questions.fact: Dew forms when moist air touches surfaces that cooled down overnight.

questions.q: What is the temperature at which air becomes full of moisture and dew forms called?
questions.fact: When the dew point is high, the air feels sticky and humid.

questions.q: What do we call balls of ice that fall from thunderstorms?
questions.fact: The largest hailstone recorded in the United States fell in South Dakota in 2010 and was about 20 centimeters wide.

questions.q: What is rain that freezes into ice pellets before reaching the ground called?
questions.fact: Sleet bounces when it hits the ground.

questions.q: What shape do snowflakes almost always have?
questions.fact: The six-sided shape comes from how water molecules link together when they freeze.

questions.q: What is a storm with strong winds and lots of blowing snow called?
questions.fact: A storm counts as a blizzard when blowing snow makes it very hard to see for hours.

questions.q: What is a long period with much less rain than usual called?
questions.fact: Droughts can dry up crops, rivers and lakes.

questions.q: What is a seasonal wind that brings heavy rains to South Asia called?
questions.fact: Farmers in India depend on monsoon rains for their crops.

questions.q: What is a violently spinning column of air that reaches from a storm cloud to the ground?
questions.fact: The fastest tornado winds can be more than 400 kilometers per hour.

questions.q: Which country has the most tornadoes in the world?
questions.fact: The United States has more than 1,000 tornadoes in a typical year.

questions.q: What is the region in the central United States known for many tornadoes?
questions.fact: Tornado Alley stretches across states like Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas.

questions.q: What is a giant spinning storm over the Atlantic Ocean with winds over 119 kilometers per hour called?
questions.fact: Hurricanes are called typhoons in the western Pacific and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.

questions.q: What is the calm area at the center of a hurricane called?
questions.fact: Inside the eye, the sky can be clear and the wind gentle, but the strongest winds surround it.

questions.q: What do hurricanes need to form?
questions.fact: Hurricanes weaken quickly after they move over land or cold water.

questions.q: Which way do hurricanes spin in the Northern Hemisphere?
questions.fact: In the Southern Hemisphere, they spin clockwise because of Earth's rotation.

questions.q: What is the effect that makes storms spin because of Earth's rotation called?
questions.fact: The Coriolis effect is too weak to decide which way water drains in a sink.

questions.q: Which weather event kills more people in the United States than tornadoes in most years?
questions.fact: Heat waves are often called the silent killer because they do not look scary.

questions.q: How hot can a lightning bolt be?
questions.fact: That is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

questions.q: About how many times does lightning strike Earth every second?
questions.fact: That adds up to about 4 million lightning strikes a day.

questions.q: Can lightning strike the same place twice?
choices: Yes, and tall buildings get hit often
questions.fact: The Empire State Building is struck by lightning about 20 times a year.

questions.q: What is the safest place to be during a thunderstorm?
choices: Inside a building or a hard-topped car
questions.fact: A good rule is when thunder roars, go indoors.

questions.q: What causes wind?
choices: Air moving from high pressure to low pressure
questions.fact: Uneven heating of Earth by the Sun creates these differences in pressure.

questions.q: What is a sea breeze?
choices: Cool wind blowing from the sea to the land on sunny days
Wind blowing from land to sea at noon
questions.fact: Land heats up faster than water, so the air over land rises and cool sea air rushes in.

questions.q: What are fast rivers of air high in the atmosphere that planes use to fly faster called?
questions.fact: Flights from the United States to Europe are often faster because of the jet stream.

questions.q: What were the steady winds that sailing ships used to cross oceans called?
questions.fact: Trade winds blow toward the equator from the east.

questions.q: What is the calm area near the equator where sailing ships often got stuck called?
questions.fact: Being in the doldrums now also means feeling bored or stuck.

questions.q: What is the hottest temperature ever recorded on Earth?
questions.fact: It was recorded in Death Valley, California, in 1913, though some scientists question the measurement.

questions.q: Where was the coldest air temperature on Earth's surface measured?
questions.fact: In 1983 it reached minus 89.2 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What is the line of latitude at 0 degrees called?
questions.fact: Places near the equator have warm weather all year.

questions.q: What is the line of longitude at 0 degrees, running through Greenwich, England, called?
questions.fact: Longitude lines run from the North Pole to the South Pole.

questions.q: What do lines of latitude measure?
choices: How far north or south of the equator a place is
How far east or west a place is
questions.fact: The North Pole is at 90 degrees north latitude.

questions.q: What happens at the North Pole in summer?
choices: It is the hottest place on Earth
The Sun stays up all day and night
questions.fact: This is why the Arctic is called the land of the midnight sun.

questions.q: What do we call the imaginary lines on a globe that help find exact locations?
questions.fact: Every place on Earth has its own latitude and longitude.

questions.q: Which line is roughly where one calendar day changes to the next?
questions.fact: It zigzags through the Pacific Ocean to avoid splitting countries.

questions.q: Is the South Pole on land or on ice floating on the ocean?
choices: On a mountain of rock with no ice
questions.fact: The ice at the South Pole is about 2,700 meters thick.

questions.q: Is the North Pole on land?
choices: No, it is on floating sea ice
questions.fact: Submarines have traveled under the ice at the North Pole.

questions.q: About how tall is Mount Everest?
questions.fact: Mount Everest is on the border between Nepal and China.

questions.q: What is the tallest mountain in Africa?
questions.fact: Kilimanjaro is a dormant volcano in Tanzania with snow near its top.

questions.q: What are the Seven Summits?
choices: The highest mountain on each continent
questions.fact: Climbing all seven is a big challenge for mountaineers.

questions.q: Which is the longest mountain range above water?
questions.fact: The Andes run about 7,000 kilometers along South America.

questions.q: What is the line above which snow stays on a mountain all year called?
questions.fact: Near the equator, the snow line is much higher than near the poles.

questions.q: What is the line on a mountain above which trees cannot grow called?
questions.fact: Above the tree line it is too cold and windy for trees.

questions.q: What are huge sheets of ice covering land, like in Antarctica and Greenland, called?
questions.fact: If all of Antarctica's ice melted, sea levels would rise by about 58 meters.

questions.q: What is a big chunk of ice that breaks off a glacier and floats in the sea called?
questions.fact: About 90 percent of an iceberg is hidden under the water.

questions.q: What is it called when a chunk of ice breaks off a glacier into the water?
questions.fact: Calving can make big splashes and even small tsunamis.

questions.q: What do we call a long period when ice sheets covered much more of Earth?
questions.fact: The last big ice age peaked about 20,000 years ago.

questions.q: What are the piles of rocks and dirt left behind by glaciers called?
questions.fact: Long Island in New York is partly made of glacier moraines.

questions.q: Which huge island is mostly covered by an ice sheet, even though its name sounds green?
questions.fact: Greenland is the world's largest island that is not a continent.

questions.q: How old is the Earth?
questions.fact: The oldest minerals found on Earth are tiny zircon crystals about 4.4 billion years old.

questions.q: What were the first living things on Earth like?
questions.fact: Simple microbes appeared at least 3.5 billion years ago.

questions.q: What were the tiny ocean microbes that first filled Earth's air with oxygen?
questions.fact: Their oxygen buildup is called the Great Oxidation Event, about 2.4 billion years ago.

questions.q: Which era is known as the Age of Dinosaurs?
questions.fact: The Mesozoic is split into the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.

questions.q: Which era are we living in now?
questions.fact: The Cenozoic Era began about 66 million years ago, after the dinosaurs died out.

questions.q: What is amber?
questions.fact: Insects trapped in amber millions of years ago can still be seen inside it.

questions.q: What is a fossil of a footprint, burrow or nest called?
questions.fact: Trace fossils tell scientists how ancient animals moved and lived.

questions.q: What does the law of superposition say about rock layers?
choices: All layers are the same age
questions.fact: It works like a pile of laundry, the bottom was put there first.

questions.q: What is soil made of?
choices: Bits of rock, rotted plants and animals, air and water
questions.fact: It can take hundreds of years to form just a few centimeters of soil.

questions.q: What is the dark, rich part of soil made from rotted plants and animals called?
questions.fact: Humus helps soil hold water and feeds plants.

questions.q: What type of soil has the tiniest particles and gets sticky when wet?
questions.fact: Clay can be shaped and baked into bricks and pottery.

questions.q: What is the best soil for growing most plants, a mix of sand, silt and clay?
questions.fact: Loam drains well but still holds enough water for roots.

questions.q: What is the solid rock under the soil called?
questions.fact: Bedrock can be just under the surface or many meters down.

questions.q: What do farmers plant to hold soil in place and stop erosion?
questions.fact: During the Dust Bowl in the 1930s, plowed prairie soil blew away in giant dust storms.

questions.q: What was the Dust Bowl?
choices: Huge dust storms on the US Great Plains in the 1930s
questions.fact: Poor farming and drought let the wind blow away tons of dry soil.

questions.q: What is the gradual warming of Earth's average temperature called?
questions.fact: As of 2025, the last ten years have been the warmest on record.

questions.q: What is the main human cause of climate change?
questions.fact: Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide that traps heat.

questions.q: Why are sea levels rising?
choices: Melting ice and warming water expanding
questions.fact: Water takes up more space as it warms.

questions.q: What thin layer of gas in the stratosphere was being damaged by chemicals called CFCs?
questions.fact: After CFCs were banned by the 1987 Montreal Protocol, the ozone layer began slowly healing.

questions.q: Over which place did a large hole in the ozone layer form each spring?
questions.fact: The ozone hole is expected to mostly recover by around 2066 over Antarctica.

questions.q: What is acid rain?
choices: Rain made acidic by pollution in the air
questions.fact: Acid rain can damage forests, lakes and stone statues.

questions.q: What is the brownish haze of air pollution over cities called?
questions.fact: The word smog was made by joining smoke and fog.

questions.q: What is it called when forests are cut down and not replaced?
questions.fact: Trees take in carbon dioxide, so cutting them down adds to climate change.

questions.q: What is planting trees where a forest was lost called?
questions.fact: A single large tree can take in more than 20 kilograms of carbon dioxide a year.

questions.q: What is the floating mass of plastic trash in the Pacific Ocean called?
questions.fact: Most of it is tiny bits of plastic, not a solid island you could walk on.

questions.q: What are the three Rs of helping the environment?
questions.fact: Reducing comes first because the best trash is the trash you never make.

questions.q: What is composting?
choices: Turning food scraps and leaves into rich soil
questions.fact: Worms and microbes do most of the work in a compost pile.

questions.q: What do we call energy from sources that will not run out, like the Sun and wind?
questions.fact: As of 2025, solar power is the fastest-growing source of electricity in the world.

questions.q: Which natural resource is formed from tiny sea creatures buried for millions of years?
questions.fact: Oil and natural gas mostly come from ancient ocean plankton.

questions.q: Where is most of Earth's liquid fresh water found?
questions.fact: Groundwater fills the spaces between rocks and soil underground.

questions.q: What do we call the process of making salt water drinkable?
questions.fact: Countries in the Middle East get much of their drinking water from desalination plants.

questions.q: What do we call water that has drained off land into rivers and streams?
questions.fact: Runoff can carry dirt and chemicals from farms and streets into rivers.

questions.q: In the water cycle, what is it called when water vapor turns into clouds?
questions.fact: The water you drink may once have been drunk by a dinosaur, because water keeps cycling.

questions.q: What powers the water cycle?
questions.fact: The Sun evaporates huge amounts of water from the oceans every day.

questions.q: What is a flood that happens very quickly, often after heavy rain, called?
questions.fact: Just 15 centimeters of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet.

questions.q: What is a sudden slide of rocks and soil down a hill called?
questions.fact: Heavy rain, earthquakes and cutting down hillside trees can cause landslides.

questions.q: What is a large mass of snow sliding fast down a mountain called?
questions.fact: Avalanches can travel more than 300 kilometers per hour.

questions.q: What is a wildfire?
questions.fact: Some trees, like certain pines, need fire's heat to open their cones and spread seeds.

questions.q: Why is Earth's magnetic field important to living things?
choices: It helps shield Earth from harmful solar particles
questions.fact: Without it, the solar wind could strip away much of the atmosphere over time.
